svg.title: What has risen is the number of people diagnosed: Taiwan, Korea and the 63-country estimate
svg.desc: A schematic in four parts, setting out what the rise in thyroid cancer looks like in different countries and where the boundaries of the idea of overdiagnosis lie. The first part is Taiwan. On the left, a line shows notified new cases of thyroid malignancy in the national cancer registry at five points: 1,228 in 1999, 2,433 in 2009, 3,737 in 2015, 4,974 in 2020 and 6,045 in 2023, roughly 4.9 times over twenty-four years. In 2023 the figures were 1,507 men and 4,538 women, and thyroid cancer ranked 11th by incidence in men and 4th in women that year. Beneath the line a note records the peer-reviewed version, which covers women only: the age-standardised incidence rate rose from 7.37 per 100,000 in 1995-1999 to 20.53 in 2015-2019, an annual percentage change of 5.9% (95% confidence interval 5.3 to 6.5), and the authors write in their conclusion that they hypothesise overdiagnosis as the main driver - a hypothesis, not an estimate. On the right, separated by a dashed rule labelled "different denominators - these two may not share an axis", is the mortality end of the same year: 225 people died of thyroid malignancy in 2023, 81 men and 144 women, 0.42% of all cancer deaths, ranked 23rd by mortality in men and 23rd in women; and this is one single year, not a trend line. The same card lists the age-standardised rates on the 2000 world standard population: age-standardised incidence 9.49 in men and 28.12 in women per 100,000, and age-standardised mortality 0.39 in men and 0.50 in women. On being diagnosed women run at roughly three times the male figure; on dying of the disease the gap is down to roughly one point three times. Below this part a crossed-out box reads "a year-by-year age-standardised mortality series for Taiwan": no officially published version was found, so the figure carries no Taiwanese mortality trend line, and the 0.39 and 0.50 cannot be used to claim that mortality has stayed flat. The second part is Korea. A line shows cases in the Korean national registry: 3,407 in 1999, 44,748 in 2012, 25,523 in 2015 and 30,676 in 2019. A note beside it records that between 1999 and 2008 incidence rose 6.4-fold (95% confidence interval 4.9 to 8.4) from 6.4 to 40.7 per 100,000, that 94.4% of the increase were tumours smaller than 20 mm and 97.1% were localised or regional disease. Below the line, three horizontal bars give age-standardised incidence per 100,000: 24.09 in 2005, 74.83 in 2012 and 42.52 in 2015, flat by 2018, with a note that people under 30 showed no significant fall after the 2015 peak and if anything signs of a further rise. Next comes a left-to-right arrow carrying two dated marks: 2012, incidence begins to fall, and 2014, the public debate begins. Beside it the figure quotes the source: the decline ran from 2012 to 2016, before the debates began in 2014; something that happened first cannot be explained by something that happened afterwards; and the curve rose again after 2015 (25,523 cases in 2015, 30,676 in 2019), so the single-line story in which one public statement brings incidence down is not drawn here. This part closes with three bars headed "deaths from thyroid cancer per 1,000 person-years among people already diagnosed with it, set out by year of diagnosis": 1.94 in 2005, 0.76 in 2013 and 2.70 in 2018, with the rise concentrated in two groups, those who had a total thyroidectomy and those who had no thyroid surgery at all. The cohort is a Korean nationwide cohort following 434,228 people already diagnosed with thyroid cancer (352,678 women, 81,550 men), mean age 48.6 years, median follow-up 7.4 years. The figure states that the denominator is people already diagnosed and not the population, a different calculation from the per-100,000 rates above, so the two lines are not comparable; in the years when screening poured large numbers of low-risk people into that denominator the mortality within this group of course fell and rose again once screening receded, so all it can speak to is that the composition of the people being diagnosed changed, and it cannot speak for the population; the authors themselves write that this line is discordant with Korean population mortality, which continuously decreased until 2015. The third part is the United States: a grey panel records that the 2025 guidelines state that between 1974 and 2013 the rise in incidence occurred across all stages, and that over the same period the mortality rate increased annually by 1.1% in advanced disease; the same document also records that after United States incidence peaked at 14.9 per 100,000 in 2015, the years 2015 to 2017 brought the first decline in three decades. So "more of it, and no more deaths" is a stronger sentence than the evidence behind it; what rebuts it is the American line, that the cell in which mortality rose is advanced disease. As for how overall mortality moved across countries, there is no series here to cite, so none is drawn. The fourth part is the 63-country estimate covering 2013 to 2017, 63 countries and 385 cancer registries. One long horizontal bar is split in two, the larger segment labelled: of 2,297,057 cases, 1,736,133 (75.6%) were attributed to overdiagnosis, of whom 1,368,181 were women and 367,952 were men. Two tags record that the female overdiagnosis fraction exceeded 85% in Cyprus, China, South Korea and Turkiye, and was estimated at zero in Uganda, Zimbabwe and Trinidad and Tobago. The same panel notes that the international gap between the highest and lowest female incidence had widened to 101.4 per 100,000 by 2012 while the international gap in mortality stayed at roughly 1.0 to 2.0 per 100,000 throughout, and it states plainly that the 75.6% is the number of people diagnosed in a whole country minus the number who would have developed symptoms, an arithmetic with no cell in it for you. A second crossed-out box below reads "a Taiwanese overdiagnosis percentage": the abstract of that paper does not name Taiwan, the full text is not open access and the supplementary material could not be obtained, so no Taiwanese overdiagnosis percentage appears on this figure and no other country is used to stand in for one. The figure ends with a red-framed panel headed "what this figure must not be read to say". Overdiagnosis is not misdiagnosis; the pathologist did not get it wrong and those really are cancer cells. Nor does it mean the thing is not really cancer; it is about whether this cancer would ever have caused trouble in this person's remaining lifetime. It can only be worked out at the level of a population and only in retrospect - the number of people diagnosed minus the number of the same people who would have developed symptoms - and no test can tell you today whether your nodule belongs to that difference. So "three-quarters of cases worldwide were attributed to overdiagnosis" cannot be rewritten as "mine probably needs no attention"; what actually decides is the histological type, the size, the invasion, the nodes on your report and your age, which are covered in "Papillary, follicular, NIFTP: reading the report" and "Why the stage depends on your age". The opposite reading is barred too: the figure does not say that finding things early is all superfluous, because mortality in the advanced-disease cell has been moving and high-risk groups were never inside the scope of the 2017 US Preventive Services Task Force grade D recommendation, which is about asymptomatic adults.

g.text: INCIDENCE, DEATHS, AND WHAT
OVERDIAGNOSIS IS NOT
What has risen is the
number of people
diagnosed
On the left, the number of new cases in Taiwan. On the
right, the number of deaths in one single year. These
are two different quantities: they do not share an axis,
and they are not subtracted from one another.
Everything on this figure is a statistic about a whole
country and a whole generation, and it can only be
worked out in retrospect. It cannot tell any one person
which kind their own nodule is.
Taiwan: the line of new cases
Notified new cases of thyroid malignancy in the national cancer registry,
from 1999 to 2023.
Notified new cases (people)
About 4.9 times over twenty-four years. In 2023: 1,507 men and
4,538 women; thyroid cancer ranked 11th by incidence in men and
4th in women that year.
The peer-reviewed version covers women only: the age-standardised
incidence rate rose from 7.37 per 100,000 in 1995-1999 to 20.53 in
2015-2019, an annual percentage change of 5.9% (95% confidence interval 5.3
to 6.5). The authors wrote in their conclusion that they "hypothesise"
overdiagnosis as the main driver - a hypothesis, not an estimate.
Different denominators - these two may not share an axis
2023, one single year
Deaths from thyroid malignancy
225 people
81 men and 144 women, 0.42% of all cancer deaths; thyroid cancer
ranked 23rd by mortality in men and 23rd in women.
National cancer registry. This is one year on its own, not a trend line.
Age-standardised rates (the age structures of different populations
are first put on one scale)
Age-standardised incidence (per 100,000)
Men 9.49 / women 28.12
Age-standardised mortality (per 100,000)
Men 0.39 / women 0.50
Standard population used
The 2000 world standard population
On being diagnosed, women run at roughly three times the male
figure. On dying of the disease, the gap between the sexes is down to
roughly one point three times. The sex ratio at the incidence end and
at the mortality end is not the same number.
A year-by-year age-standardised mortality series for Taiwan
No officially published version was found. So this figure carries no
Taiwanese mortality trend line: the 0.39 and 0.50 above are one single
year, and cannot be used to say that mortality "has stayed flat".
Korea: the curve, and its real chronology
Korea is the most thoroughly studied example, and the one most often
retold as a single-line cause and effect.
Cases in the Korean national registry (people)
Between 1999 and 2008 incidence rose 6.4-fold (95% confidence
interval 4.9 to 8.4), from 6.4 to 40.7 per 100,000. Of the increase,
94.4% were tumours smaller than 20 mm and 97.1% were localised
or regional disease.
Age-standardised incidence (per 100,000)
Flat by 2018. And in people under 30 there was no significant fall
after the 2015 peak; if anything there are signs of a further rise.
The chronology does not line up
incidence begins to fall
the public debate begins
The paper says it plainly: the decline ran from 2012 to 2016, before
the debates began in 2014. Something that happened first cannot be
explained by something that happened afterwards.
And the curve rose again after 2015: 25,523 cases in 2015, 30,676 in
2019. So the single-line story - one public statement, and incidence
falls - is not drawn here.
Deaths from thyroid cancer per 1,000 person-years among people
already diagnosed with it, set out by year of diagnosis
The rise was concentrated in two groups: those who had a total
thyroidectomy, and those who had no thyroid surgery at all. In the
years when screening poured large numbers of low-risk people into
that denominator, mortality within this group of course fell; when
screening receded it rose again. All it can speak to is that the
composition of the people being diagnosed changed. It cannot speak
for the population. The authors write that this line is discordant with
Korean population mortality, which continuously decreased until
A Korean nationwide cohort followed 434,228 people already diagnosed with
thyroid cancer (352,678 women, 81,550 men), mean age 48.6 years, median
follow-up 7.4 years. The denominator is people already diagnosed, not the
population; it is a different calculation from the per-100,000 rates above, and
the two lines are not comparable.
"Mortality did not move at all" is also
wrong, and only the US sentence rebuts it
From 1974 to 2013, mortality in advanced disease rose by 1.1% a year
The 2025 guidelines put it this way: over that period the rise in
incidence occurred across all stages, and over the same period the
mortality rate increased annually by 1.1% in advanced disease.
The same document also records that after United States incidence
peaked at 14.9 per 100,000 in 2015, the years 2015 to 2017 brought
the first decline in three decades.
So "more of it, and no more deaths" is a stronger sentence than the
evidence behind it. What rebuts it is the American line: the cell in
which mortality rose is advanced disease. As for how overall
mortality moved across countries, there is no series here to cite, so
none is drawn.
The 63-country estimate, and why Taiwan
is not in it
The largest estimate available covers 2013 to 2017, 63 countries and 385
cancer registries.
Of 2,297,057 cases, 1,736,133 (75.6%) were attributed
to overdiagnosis
Attributed to overdiagnosis: 1,736,133 cases (75.6%)
The remaining cases
Of those, 1,368,181 were women and 367,952 were men.
Above 85% in women: Cyprus, China, South Korea, Turkiye
Estimated at zero: Uganda, Zimbabwe, Trinidad and Tobago
The same paper offers one more contrast: the international gap
between the highest and lowest female incidence had widened to
101.4 per 100,000 by 2012, while the international gap in mortality
stayed at roughly 1.0 to 2.0 per 100,000 throughout.
That 75.6% is the number of people diagnosed in a whole country
minus the number who would have developed symptoms. There is no
cell in that arithmetic for you.
A Taiwanese overdiagnosis percentage
The abstract of that paper does not name Taiwan, the full text is not open
access and the supplementary material could not be obtained. So no
Taiwanese overdiagnosis percentage appears on this figure, and no other
country's figure is used to stand in for one.
What this figure must not be read to say
Overdiagnosis is not misdiagnosis. The pathologist did not
get it wrong; those really are cancer cells.
Nor does overdiagnosis mean "it is not really cancer". It is
about whether this cancer would ever have caused trouble
in this person's remaining lifetime, not about whether the
diagnosis is correct.
It can only be worked out at the level of a population, and
only in retrospect: the number of people diagnosed, minus
the number of the same people who would have developed
symptoms. No test can tell you today whether your nodule
belongs to that difference.
So "three-quarters of cases worldwide were attributed to
overdiagnosis" cannot be rewritten as "mine probably
needs no attention". What actually decides is the histological
type, the size, the invasion, the nodes on your report, and
your age - those are in "Papillary, follicular, NIFTP: reading
the report" and "Why the stage depends on your age".
The opposite reading is barred too: this figure does not say
that finding things early is all superfluous. Mortality in the
advanced-disease cell has been moving, and high-risk
groups were never inside the scope of the 2017 US
Preventive Services Task Force grade D recommendation -
that recommendation is about asymptomatic adults.
Schematic, redrawn from the Republic of China 2023 Cancer
Registry Annual Report, the Korean national registry and nationwide
cohort studies, the 2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines for
differentiated thyroid cancer and the 63-country overdiagnosis
estimate; not reproduced from the figures of the original papers. The
cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the
data points must not be compared directly.
